item.title: Monsoon ends with 12.6% rainfall deficit, driest season in a decade
item.description: The rains in eastern and northeastern states were the lowest since 1901, the weather department said.
item.content:encoded:
The southwest monsoon ended on Wednesday with a 12.6% deficit in rainfall, said the India Meteorological Department. This makes the season the driest in 11 years and the fourth driest in this century.

The southwest monsoon had set in on June, 4 marking the beginning of the four-month rainy season in the country. This year, the monsoon arrived three days later than its usual onset date of June 1.

It covered the entire country on July 9, a day later than the normal date of July 8.

On Wednesday, the IMD said that the country had received 759.4 mm of rainfall against the long-period average of 868.6 mm.

The long-period average is the measure of the mean rainfall during the four-month monsoon season over the last 50 years.

The weather department further said that monsoon rainfall over northwest India was 94.1% of the long-period average, over central India it was 97%, over the southern Peninsula it was 74% and over the North East, it was 74%.

At 1,017.1 mm, the rainfall in eastern and northeastern states was the lowest since 1901. During a press conference, the IMD also pointed out that the average rainfall received by northeastern states has been showing a consistent decline.

item.title: Indian women are on the streets again. Everything has changed but nothing has changed
item.description: Women are no longer petitioning for safety but claiming their right to public spaces. Yet, the rest of the country seems willfully ignorant.
item.content:encoded:
September has seen an avalanche of reported attacks against women and girls. I use the word “reported” because there is always more violence than is reported at any time and private violence tends to be invisibilised.

I want to write. To say something. I stare at my computer screen. Nothing. I try sitting with a pen and paper but the paper stays blank. What do I even write that someone, perhaps even I, have not said before?

It seems impossible that in 2026 we are still having the same conversations and the context is, if anything, more misogynist than when we started out a three-year project researching women’s access to public space in 2003.

We were not the only ones asking questions about gendered public space. On this journey we met Jasmeen Patheja, student at the Shrishti School of Design working on street sexual harassment, a project titled Blank Noise, a project that became a campaign. With her, we staged an intervention on the streets following the rape perpetrated by a police constable on Marine Drive in 2005.

Thousands of women gathered at Delhi University’s North Campus after the alleged gangrape of a 17-year-old girl.

Patrick Branco Ruivo would leave his role at the end of the year after an internal probe found “operational flaws and shortcomings” in organising the visit had led to the “unacceptable” removal of the women staff, the news agency quoted the firm, Société d’exploitation de la Tour Eiffel, as saying.

On September 7, the staff at the monument went on a brief strike to protest the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a delegation of the Hindu denomination Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha two days earlier.

The removal of the women staff had sparked criticism from French politicians across the spectrum, who said that the country’s values about gender equality were not negotiable.

item.title: Flydubai incident: What we know so far
item.description: The airline said the reason for the Indian pilot being stabbed by his co-pilot was unknown. Netanyahu claimed that the pilot saved the plane from being crashed.
item.content:encoded:
The Flydubai pilot who was allegedly stabbed by his co-pilot during a flight to Israel on Wednesday is Indian.

Although Flydubai has stated that “the underlying reasons behind this event are unknown” at this stage, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that the co-pilot had been trying to crash the plane and kill its passengers. Out of the 174 passengers onboard, 166 were Israeli, reported AFP.

The flight, which took off from Dubai early on Wednesday, sent an emergency signal about two hours into the flight, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24. Minutes later, the signal indicated a possible hijacking before being changed to a general emergency alert.

The plane had plummeted about 17,000 feet in altitude in a minute. It landed safely at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

item.title: An artist who thought cinematically: What Tyeb Mehta’s drawings and sketches say about his art
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Tyeb Mehta: Bearing Weight with the Lightness of Being Art’, edited by Roobina Karode and Srinivas Aditya Mopidevi.
item.content:encoded:
For Tyeb Mehta, the line was never merely a formal device. It carried philosophical and emotional weight, embodying memory, myth, pain and redemption, with an intensity that was both provocative and contemplative. It is through his drawings that we trace the paradox at the heart of his practice: that the instability we perceive on his canvases was carefully engineered.

Mehta’s drawings have piqued visitors to the retrospective Tyeb Mehta: Bearing Weight (with the lightness of being). Largely unseen for decades, they facilitate fresh curatorial perspectives on his visual language. We seldom see an artist’s preliminary exercises or the evolutionary charting of a creative practice. Such materials are often misplaced or lost after an artist’s death. Our access to the Tyeb Mehta Foundation’s archive, which has been preserved and catalogued with great care, allowed us to work backwards to the origins of tropes and motifs that recurred through his career.

Mehta’s early drawings reveal an artist deeply invested in form and demonstrate the experiments he undertook to break and contort this form from within, long before these concerns found their fullest expression in his paintings. His association with members of the Progressive Artists’ Group further propelled him towards developing a distinctly modernist language, rooted not in imitation...

The police had detained Abdul Barek, a resident of Gopalpur village, in June.

The family told Scroll that the police had ignored that Barek’s name was on the electoral rolls after the special intensive revision exercise was conducted in the state and had voted in the Assembly elections held in May. item.title: ‘No one to protect us’: In Manipur, civilians easy targets as armed groups step up violence
item.description: At least 23 unarmed people have been killed in 30 days in ongoing Naga-Kuki conflict. Residents say the government is missing in action.
item.content:encoded:
The Sunday church service had just ended in the hill-top village of Longpi in Manipur’s Noney district on the afternoon of September 13.

Longpi is home to about 320 Kuki residents, village officials said.

A group of five women and two men were on their way to gather some rice and wash some clothes when a group of 45-50 militants attacked the village.

“They were walking from one part of the village to another when they came under attack,” David Gangte, the son of Longpi village chief and a primary school government teacher at the village, told Scroll.

Gangte said the group found themselves cornered in a narrow lane when the militants opened fire with “automatic weapons”.

Two people – Thangvel Roel Gangte, 43, and Julie Singson 22 – were killed on the spot. Singson was two months pregnant at the time. Another 22-year-old woman, Ester Gangte, sustained severe bullet injuries and died later in a hospital in Churachandpur, about 250 km away.

They were not the only civilians to have lost their lives in a deadly surge of violence in Manipur.

item.title: Rohingya genocide: ICJ will soon issue ruling on case against Myanmar
item.description: The ruling could strengthen the case for a formal recognition from Myanmar of the Rohingya and the restitution of their citizenship rights.
item.content:encoded:
The International Court of Justice is reportedly going to rule in the coming weeks in The Gambia v. Myanmar, the genocide case against Myanmar.

In 2019, The Gambia filed an application at the ICJ alleging that Myanmar had violated the United Nations’ 1948 Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya people.

The Rohingya aren’t from The Gambia, and no atrocities against them took place there. But, under international law, any state can file a case with the ICJ if it believes a country has violated the convention. This was confirmed by the court in a 2022 decision against Myanmar’s attempt to block the case on jurisdictional grounds.

Who are the Rohingya?

The Rohingya are an ethnic minority group that have long lived in the Arakan region of western Myanmar, which today corresponds to the Rakhine state.

As Muslims in an overwhelmingly Buddhist country, the Rohingya have often experienced discrimination and persecution. Most notably, in 1982, Myanmar passed a law that removed the Rohingya from a list of ethnic groups eligible for citizenship.

As a result, most Rohingya lost their citizenship, and with it, their most basic rights and freedoms. The ICJ case, however, concerns the campaign of violence conducted by the Myanmar military against the Rohingya that began in 2016.

item.title: Arunachal: Vehicle torched, MLA’s home vandalised during protests against Siang dam
item.description: The protests were held during Chief Minister Pema Khandu’s visit to a town in Upper Siang district.
item.content:encoded:
Protests by residents of the Siang basin in Arunachal Pradesh against a proposed multipurpose dam intensified on Wednesday, as demonstrators clashed with security personnel and set a police vehicle on fire during Chief Minister Pema Khandu’s visit to Yingkiong in Upper Siang district, the Hindustan Times reported.

Residents of the Siang basin have opposed the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project for several years. Members of the Adi tribe, who live in the basin, have maintained that the project threatens their land and way of life. The protests intensified after the government began deploying Central Armed Police Forces for the pre-feasibility survey of the proposed project.

The Siang river flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, and is the main tributary of the Brahmaputra. The river is the site of the proposed 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, described to be India’s largest dam.

On Monday, villagers and security personnel clashed in Geku during protests against the project and the deployment of Central Armed Police Forces for the pre-feasibility survey, Arunachal24 reported. Four persons were arrested in connection with the incident.

As tensions rose on Wednesday, protesters allegedly entered and vandalised the residence of Tuting-Yingkiong MLA Alo Libang in Yingkiong. Several government vehicles were also reportedly damaged.

item.title: Eggs, chicken could cost more as maize shortage due to ethanol blending will worsen amid poor rain
item.description: Nearly three-fourths of the ethanol produced in India currently comes from grains, particularly maize.
item.content:encoded:
Despite a record maize production last year, India’s poultry farmers are contending with higher retail prices of the poultry staple due to its increasing demand for ethanol blending. With a decline in sowing and deficient rainfall this year, experts say this is likely to get worse.

Maize was available to poultry farmers for Rs 12-14 per kg around the year 2019 but it now sells for Rs 27- Rs 28 per kg in the retail market. Since maize is the primary, starch-heavy food for all poultry and soymeal is the secondary food, farmers maintaining egg-layer and broiler poultry are both facing a crisis. They have to buy feed at these high prices and either pass on the cost to the consumer or bear the losses.

The contribution of maize towards ethanol blending increased from 0% in 2021-’22 to around 37% in 2025-26. India’s move to blend 20% ethanol in petrol has been a subject of much discussion this past year after vehicle owners alleged damage due to the biofuel. Besides, when sugar prices surged recently, it led to debate on whether it was due to the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme.

Six party workers were also arrested, the newspaper quoted an Agra Police statement as saying.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘How to Date a Fanatic’, by Aruni Kashyap.

Karan drove me home since we both lived in the University Enclave: the same place where I had spent the best years of my life after moving to Delhi to study for university. As I sat in his car and watched the city through the windows, I remembered how I had marvelled at those neem trees and those red brick buildings when I first arrived in the city as an undergraduate, and how much I now missed those happy, carefree days. I wasn’t unhappy now. Yes, Dhruv refused to date me, and I had spent the last several months loving him from across a border I didn’t have the passport to cross. Still, I had spent the past few weeks going to a therapist, trying to be comfortable in my skin, and now, accepting Dhruv’s rejection. I wasn’t prepared for such intense pain. I was writing poems. Bad poems. And I had never written poems about anything – not even a flower.

item.title: SP fields Reliance executive Dhanraj Nathwani as Rajya Sabha candidate from Uttar Pradesh

The Samajwadi Party on Wednesday fielded Reliance Industries executive Dhanraj Nathwani as one of its two candidates for the Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh.

Dhanraj Nathwani is group president at the Mukesh Ambani-led conglomerate and a director at Reliance New Energy Limited and Reliance Projects and Property Management Services Limited, according to his LinkedIn profile.

He is the son of four-time Rajya Sabha MP Parimal Nathwani, who was re-elected from Jharkhand as a National Democratic Alliance-backed independent in June. Parimal Nathwani is also the director of corporate affairs at Reliance Industries.

Dhanraj Nathwani has been vice-president of the Gujarat Cricket Association since September 2019. He has previously held positions in the Jamnagar District Football Association and other institutions in Gujarat.

On Wednesday, SP chief Akhilesh Yadav said that the party decided to connect with the industrial sector because several political parties have a presence in the corporate world.

“I am delighted that the Samajwadi Party has been given the opportunity to send a person from a new generation,” he said.

The party’s other candidate is Ram Gopal Yadav, Akhilesh Yadav’s uncle and a Rajya Sabha member since 2008.

In a recently liberated economy characterised by speed, the commodification of women's bodies and consumerist culture, Bhashwati is an increasingly disillusioned misfit who has, ironically, just started working in an advertising firm. But her life changes one day when she finds out about the mysterious Mohua Roy, a former copywriter with the company, whose desk Bhashwati now uses. The company employees remain tight-lipped about Mohua, who had left abruptly for reasons unknown. On finding a poem written by Mohua, Bhashwati decides to search for her. item.title: The Indian state has made Bengali Muslims outsiders in their own land
item.description: Documents are meaningless with ethno-linguistic identity reason enough for arbitrary detention and even deportation of marginal workers across India.
item.content:encoded:
Reading news reports in recent weeks has made one thing clear: being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has, by itself, become incriminating in today’s India.

Simply having this ethno-linguistic identity is enough to trigger the suspicion of state officials. Amid the fervid political rhetoric about “ghuspetiya” – infiltrators – and supposed demographic change, being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has come to be associated with being an outsider.

Across the country, Bengali-speaking Muslim marginal workers are being picked up for questioning, detained and even deported to Bangladesh. For instance, last month in Bengaluru, 3,000-odd Bengali Muslim garbage and waste workers were picked up by the police as part of a massive verification drive against allegedly unauthorised migrants.

Only 31 of them were eventually determined to be Bangladeshi nationals and sent to West Bengal to be deported to Bangladesh. In Chhattisgarh, 23 workers from West Bengal – only one Hindu and the rest Muslims – were detained on suspicion of being Bangladeshi nationals this month.

In July, a Muslim woman tracing her roots to North 24 Parganas district of West Bengal was detained and deported to Bangladesh in July.

The suicide bombing and gun attack that killed dozens in northwest Pakistan on September 18, 2026, highlighted the fragile security situation in the South Asian country. But it also shone a light on the complex and evolving extremism landscape there and the strained relationship between Pakistan and neighboring Afghanistan.

The assault took place as worshipers gathered for Friday prayers in the city of Kohat, in Khyber Puktunkhwa province, northwest Pakistan. A suicide bomber rammed an explosives-laden car through the wall of a police complex in the city of Kohat, targeting the mosque inside. Gunmen then exchanged fire with law enforcement officials during a 20-hour standoff. In all, 31 people were killed, including 16 police officers, while over 100 people were reported injured.

Supporters of the militant group Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, or IMP, claimed responsibility on encrypted apps like Telegram. But other seemingly aligned groups distanced themselves from the attack. Pakistan responded by conducting airstrikes in Afghanistan, home to at least one of the gunmen.

item.title: A new self-help book argues that ‘fake it till you make it’ actually works
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Be Delusional: Bend Reality to Your Beliefs’, by Harinder Singh Pelia.
item.content:encoded:
Has it ever happened to you that you ask someone who they are, and first they give you some random labels, then they start telling you even more random stories? Like, I am a senior manager of random things at Random Pvt. Ltd, and then, the moment you make the mistake of becoming slightly comfortable, they launch into a story of their childhood. Let’s admit it: we’ve all done a version of this at some point. There is a collection of stories we carry within us only to tell other people, but there is also a larger collection we hold to tell ourselves.

Psychologist Dan McAdams has spent all his life figuring out the stories people tell themselves and others. item.title: Beyond the myth of India’s Sanskrit-speaking villages, can the language anchor modern life?
item.description: To truly revitalise a language, it must belong to the messy, everyday realities of its speakers.

For over two decades, an extraordinary cultural and political experiment has unfolded along the mist-shrouded slopes of the Himalayas. The state government of Uttarakhand set out to construct a network of saṃskṛta-grāms – dedicated “Sanskrit-speaking” villages designed to transform the region into a living, breathing Sanskrit wonderland. Crores of rupees were poured into local administrations with a bold vision: resurrecting the “Language of the Gods” from its classical and liturgical repose and embedding it into the soil of everyday rural Indian life.

Yet, year after year, this ambitious policy narrative undergoes a curious ritual of its own.It is repeatedly re-released, temporarily mobilising ideological enthusiasts, only to stall amid bureaucratic quietude and persistent allegations of corruption. item.title: Is calisthenics an effective form of exercise or just another fitness fad?
item.description: Learning to move your own body, control it and gradually make it stronger is one of the simplest, cheapest ways to start training.
item.content:encoded:
Calisthenics has gained enormous popularity in recent years, particularly thanks to social media and the rise of workout areas in city parks. You probably know some of the moves already, like pull-ups, push-ups, dips and squats.

For the more advanced, it also includes eye-catching, gravity-defying moves like the muscle-up, planche (where the body is held horizontal, supported solely by the hands) or the front lever (where the body is held horizontally while hanging from a bar).

But is calisthenics an effective form of exercise, or just another fitness fad? To answer this question, we first need to clarify what it is.

Calisthenics is a form of training that mainly uses a person’s own body weight as resistance. Its name derives from the Greek terms kállos (“beautiful”) and sthenos (“strength”), though the word’s modern use only caught on during the 19th century, when it referred to various forms of physical exercise.

Today, it includes well-known exercises such as squats, lunges, push-ups, pull-ups and dips, but calisthenics is not inherently acrobatic. Anyone who starts by doing a simple wall push-up is using the same principle as someone doing a one-arm push-up on the ground: moving their body against gravity.

item.title: Literary tourism: Why the places we love in books can never quite be found in real life
item.description: Literary geography, which combines physical geography with literary studies, emerged as the novel became popular and grew alongside literary tourism.
item.content:encoded:
From the Brontës’ Haworth to Jane Austen’s Bath, Wordsworth’s Lake District and Thomas Hardy’s Dorset, literary places continue to exert a powerful hold over readers.

Literary tourism appears to be enjoying renewed popularity, from visits inspired by classic novels to the TikTok trend of turning books into travel itineraries. But what exactly are literary tourists hoping to find when they get there? The answer is more complicated than it might seem.

Haworth, Bath and Dorset all exist, obviously. They can be found on a map and visited. But the Brontë moors, Austen’s Bath, Wordsworth’s Lakes and Hardy’s Wessex are also literary reimaginings of those places. They may never have existed in quite the form readers imagine.

Our fascination with literary places has a long history. Literary geography, which combines physical geography with literary studies, emerged in the late 19th century as the novel grew in popularity and, in many ways, grew alongside literary tourism.

In 1899, William Lyon Phelps created his Literary Map of England, marking locations associated with authors and literary works. A few years later, William Sharp’s Literary Geography (1904) mapped regions such as “Dickens land”, “the Brontë country” and the literary geography of the English lakes.

Since Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran in February, plunging the Gulf region into conflict, the countries have also been waging an information war using tools powered by artificial intelligence. To separate fact from fiction, authorities, analysts, and journalists alike turned to commercial satellite imagery, including Google Earth, the closest thing to “ground truth,” with limited access to sites.

Google Earth has long been a trusted infrastructure for the verification field, and is the platform on which open-source investigators are formally trained for conflict work in Syria, Yemen, and Sudan. item.title: ‘Dance is my breathing, my survival, my everything’: Mohiniattam exponent Sunanda Nair
item.description: In August, Nair received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in the Overseas category for 2024 – the first recipient of the honour.
item.content:encoded:
For 62-year-old Sunanda Nair, the journey from the Mumbai suburb of Goregaon to the world stage was never mapped out as a career plan. But dance simply kept opening doors.

Nair began learning bharatanatyam when she was six, took up kathakali a few years later and eventually found her artistic identity in mohiniattam.

In between, she became the first student in India to earn a bachelor’s degree (in 1989) and master’s (in 1991) in this dance form practised in Keralam. Then Nair upgraded to a doctorate (2016) with a thesis titled “The Intrinsic Lyrical Feminism in Mohini Attam” at Mumbai’s Nalanda Nritya Kala Mahavidyalaya. where she learnt dance, taught and discovered herself.

When Nair moved to the US in 2000 because her husband got a job there, she did not arrive with a mission to establish herself as a performer or teacher. In fact, she thought she might stop dancing altogether. Instead, students came looking for her. Performances followed. An accidental new start grew into a sustained effort to teach, perform and present an Indian classical form to American audiences without diluting its character.

item.title: The bid to improve safety in public parks cannot involve keeping the public out
item.description: Rather than rushing in with stopgap fixes, the authorities must nurture a sense of ownership and respond to the concerns and needs of communities.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, a 17-year-old was allegedly gang raped in a public park in Delhi by three men claiming to be from the police. Her 17-year-old male friend was beaten. The three men are reported to have told the friends that they faced potential legal trouble, separated them and then sexually assaulted the girl.

As the attack sparked concerns about safety in public parks in the national capital, the Delhi Development Authority said it would restrict entry to these spaces after sunset, install security cameras at the gates and increase surveillance by the police and security guards.

It added that it would conduct a safety audit of the 600 parks that it manages.

To some, this sounds reasonable. If the safety audit finds that a particular park cannot be kept secure after dark, restricting access could be an acceptable temporary solution.

But if a public space is deemed to be unsafe, is the way to make it safer actually to keep the public out?

Cities such as Delhi already suffer from a paucity of accessible open spaces, where young people can meet their friends, couples can spend time together and residents can walk, exercise, play a sport – or simply just sit and stare.

item.title: One hundred years of Mahasweta Devi: Stories of subaltern heroes who live on in memory
item.description: Devi had once said that ‘a responsible writer, standing at a turning point in history, has to take a stand in defence of the exploited.’
item.content:encoded:
Picture a classroom in rural India. The textbook chapter on the freedom struggle lists your regular names – Gandhi, Nehru, Bose, Patel – with familiar photographs. In such a setting, it’s natural that a young tribal girl once asked Mahasweta Devi, “When we go to school, we read about Mahatma Gandhi. Did we have no heroes? Did we always suffer like this?”

The question assumes its own answer. If your stories aren’t told, your gods are not worshipped in temples, your warriors are not commemorated in statues, then perhaps – or so the logic goes – you had no stories, no gods, no warriors.

Just like how they inspire millions, stories can also disempower millions. India has always had a strange relationship with its stories and mythologies. Our mythologies afflict the afflicted, uplift the uplifted. They maintain the status quo, console the powerful, and justify caste and gender hierarchies.

In this land of the high and mighty, of the divinely chosen, of victors writing the stories of victories, lived Mahasweta Devi. In the preface to Jhansir Rani, Devi writes, “Those who usurped the throne also controlled the pen. item.title: Since BJP victory, Bengal’s Christians have faced at least 35 attacks, disruptions of prayer service
item.description: Instead of action being taken against the perpetrators, it is the victims who are often taken to police stations, community leaders say.
item.content:encoded:
In the hinterland of Bengal, mostly hidden from the attention of the mainstream media, Hindutva outfits are mounting a sustained assault against small Christian communities.

Since the Bharatiya Janata Party assumed power in West Bengal in May, these minority communities have faced rising hostility. Hindutva outfits and fringe groups have attacked community members, disrupted church services and vandalised churches, frequently alleging forced conversion or proselytisation as justification for the harassment and violence.

The police have registered FIRs in several of these incidents, but no action has been taken against the perpetrators. Instead, victims are being taken to police stations, said Herod Mullick, founder of the Bangiya Christiya Pariseba or Bengal Christian Council.

“Over the past two-and-a-half to three months, such incidents have increased across districts, following a similar pattern,” Mullick told Alt News. “We have repeatedly sought a meeting with the chief minister, demanding an impartial investigation. But the government is not paying heed. So many people are being beaten, crosses are being broken, and someone or the other is being subjected to harassment every other day. item.title: Instead of pushing hard at exercise, try ‘slow jogging’
item.description: Exercise does not have to be intense to improve health.
item.content:encoded:
Avid runners are often chasing speed. Whether that’s improving their 5K or shaving seconds off their marathon time to nail a personal best. The idea that exercise should involve pushing further, harder or faster has long been embedded in fitness culture.

But against this backdrop, some people have adopted the almost counter-cultural belief that the key to fitness is to take things slow.

The growing popularity of the “slow jogging” trend online counters a lot of what we’ve been taught about fitness. Rather than striving for speed, the slow jogging trend encourages people to take short steps and move at a pace slow enough to comfortably hold a conversation.

To some people, this might look too easy to count as exercise. But exercise does not have to be intense to improve health.

The slow jogging trend was originally developed by a Japanese researcher named Hiroaki Tanaka. According to the researcher, jogging at “niko-niko pace” which translates to “smiling pace”) could be a more enjoyable way to improve cardiovascular fitness. The trend eventually caught on in South Korea before going viral online, where it is now being adopted by people all around the world.

item.title: ‘The Disappearers’: Marlon James’s new novel gives voice to the gay men Jamaica erased
item.description: The Booker Prize-longlisted novel reveals the varied and intimate realities of gay men, their backstories, and afterlives.
item.content:encoded:
Marlon James’s 2026 novel, The Disappearers, has already been hailed as the novel of the century by The New York Times, and it is certainly magnificent and explosive in equal measure. Its success lies in the way its artistic execution dovetails with its highly charged subject matter.

The Disappearers pulls the reader into a seemingly knowable time and place – the Jamaica of 1988 to 2005. Yet what James seeks to make known and felt is not to be found in any record or archive. Focusing on the experiences of men who love, desire, and have sex with men in a virulently homophobic Jamaican society, this is a novel that explores a silenced history with astonishing depth and detail.

In my own work, I have published literary criticism that argues for the Caribbean as a constitutively queer, as well as a homophobic, space and I found The Disappearers to be a powerful literary reckoning with this hidden past. item.title: A gallery of memories: How Kolkata’s citizens are preserving the city’s Chinese heritage
item.description: The Cheenapara Heritage Gallery in Tiretta Bazar is part of an urban revival initiative that also aims to revive the Chinese neighbourhood’s food streets.
item.content:encoded:
A menu from the 1960s from Waldorf Restaurant, located on Russell Street. A bottle of Pou Chong’s sauce, established in a factory in Tangra.

These are among the artefacts on display at the Cheenapara Heritage Gallery, which opened its doors in Kolkata’s Tiretta Bazar on September 5 to showcase the rich heritage of the city’s Chinese community.

“We need a place to keep, preserve, document, and showcase all of it to not just the Chinese community but also Kolkata’s citizens at large,” said Sohini Pyne, a conservation architect and curator of the gallery. “Those who live in Kolkata must know the Chinese history of the city and the intimate stories of these spaces.”

item.title: ‘Good Arguments’: Playwright Deepika Arwind’s first novel for adults is fresh and fiercely feminist
item.description: The novel captures the essence of being a young woman trying to build a life in the arts while learning to navigate newly discovered adult worlds.
item.content:encoded:
Deepika Arwind’s Good Arguments is an ambitious work of fiction that captures the multitudinous realities of women living in urban spaces in India. Through the story of the protagonist, 20-something Delphi Rodriguez, Arwind captures the essence of being a young woman trying to build a life in the arts while learning to navigate newly discovered adult worlds. Set in the early 2010s, the novel follows Delphi as she begins to forge her own identity while attempting to decode the theatre scene in Bangalore, a space in which both her class and her gender make her an outsider.

Delphi is freshly out of college when she lands a role in an intensive theatre training programme run by Laila, a renowned director in the theatre community.
